title: She Will Break the All-Time Record on Sunday. Her Response to the Retirement Question Was Three Words.
excerpt: Harmanpreet Kaur leads India into the Women's T20 World Cup in England, where the opening match against Pakistan at Edgbaston will draw the largest Indian diaspora crowd in tournament history.
body:
When a reporter asked Harmanpreet Kaur last week whether this would be her final T20 World Cup, the Indian captain did not offer a diplomatic non-answer. She turned the question back: *"Why? You think I should stop?"*

The exchange, filmed during India's pre-tournament press conference, went viral within hours. It also told you everything about where the 37-year-old stands heading into the tenth edition of the ICC Women's T20 World Cup, which begins in England on June 12.

By stepping onto the field in Birmingham on Sunday, when India face Pakistan in their opening Group A fixture at Edgbaston, Harmanpreet will surpass New Zealand's Suzie Bates for the most appearances in women's international cricket history. She has been part of India's T20 World Cup squad since the very first edition in 2009. This will be the fifth time she captains the side at the tournament.

## India's Settled Batting, Unsettled Bowling

India arrive as the reigning ODI World Cup champions, having won the 50-over trophy earlier this year. The T20 version, however, has been a different story. India reached the final in 2020, lost in the semi-finals in 2023, and were eliminated in the group stage in 2024. Across formats, there is no team in women's cricket with a bigger gap between the quality of its batting and the fragility of its bowling.

The batting lineup is formidable. Smriti Mandhana, the vice-captain, has an exceptional record in English conditions — her county stint and previous series in England have given her the kind of comfort on those surfaces that few Indian batters, men or women, possess. Aakash Chopra, previewing the tournament, called Mandhana and Shafali Verma India's "biggest X-factors," arguing that the team's fortunes rest on how aggressively the opening pair attacks during the Powerplay.

Behind them, Jemimah Rodrigues offers adaptability at three or four, and Richa Ghosh provides the finishing power. Bharti Fulmali, who scored an unbeaten fifty in the warm-up win over West Indies in Cardiff last week, gives the middle order depth.

The bowling, though, is a concern. Injuries to Amanjot Kaur and Kashvee Gautam have thinned India's pace options. Renuka Singh Thakur will carry the workload, supported by Nandni Sharma, the uncapped Chandigarh pacer who earned her call-up after claiming 17 wickets in the Women's Premier League. The spin department — Deepti Sharma, Shreyanka Patil, Shree Charani, and the returning Radha Yadav — is India's stronger suit, and on English surfaces that assist turn, it could be decisive.

## Pakistan at Edgbaston: More Than a Cricket Match

India's opening fixture against Pakistan at Edgbaston on June 14 carries weight far beyond the result. Birmingham has one of the largest South Asian populations of any city in the United Kingdom. Community organisations from Leicester, Coventry, and the broader West Midlands have already sold out group bookings. For NRIs in the UK, this is the most accessible women's cricket event in memory — no flights to Dubai or South Africa, no late-night time zones. The stadium is a bus ride away.

The rivalry has history. India have dominated the head-to-head record in T20 World Cups, but Pakistan's bowling attack, led by Fatima Sana, has the pace and swing to exploit English conditions early. Sadia Iqbal and Nashra Sandhu can turn the ball sharply. If England's skies cooperate, this match could be the most competitive India-Pakistan women's fixture in years.

## The Road Ahead

India's group also includes Australia, South Africa, Bangladesh, and the Netherlands. Australia at Lord's on June 28 is the marquee fixture, but the South Africa match on June 21 at Old Trafford could determine whether India finish in the top two. India lost the recent T20I series to South Africa 1-4, and that result lingers.

For Harmanpreet, the calculation is straightforward. India have won every ICC trophy available in women's cricket *except* the T20 World Cup. In 2020, they reached the final and froze. In 2023, they lost a semi-final by five runs. A title in England, where the diaspora can fill the stands, would complete the set — and make retirement questions permanently irrelevant.
